lessonPlan.title: The Goophered Grapevine unit
lessonPlan.author: Charles W. Chesnutt
lessonPlan.edition: First published: The Atlantic Monthly, Aug 1887
lessonPlan.editionNote: Reading text: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Conjure_Woman/The_Goophered_Grapevine (revision 14117353), cleaned for Liber et Libri.
lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 10–12 (scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Goophered Grapevine.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Goophered Grapevine: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

lessonPlan.middleSchoolTrack: Short story: read whole in one 90-minute lesson (assign longer stories as pre-reading). Middle School prompts use the full text when the grade tags include 6–8; otherwise teacher-selected passages.
lessonPlan.schedule: One 90-minute lesson (the whole story), with an optional take-home essay
essentialQuestions: What does The Goophered Grapevine suggest about slavery and its memory?
What does The Goophered Grapevine suggest about storytelling as resistance?
What does The Goophered Grapevine suggest about race and economics?
objectives: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly and implicitly.
Determine themes and analyze their development over the course of the story.
Analyze how characters, setting and point of view interact.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in the text.
Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.

wholeBookTest.title: The Goophered Grapevine: whole-book test

items.prompt: Why does John come to North Carolina?
options: To fight in a war
To teach
His wife needs a milder climate and he seeks a business
To visit family

items.prompt: Who tells the tale of the vineyard?
options: The narrator's wife
Aunt Peggy
Uncle Julius McAdoo
Henry
A ghost
A conjure spell
A kind of grape
A plantation tool

items.prompt: What happens to Henry with the seasons?
options: He becomes free
He escapes north
He grows young and strong with the vines, then weak
He is sold

items.prompt: What does John suspect about Julius's story?
options: Julius was afraid
Julius wanted to buy the land
Julius profited from the grapes and wanted to keep them
It was all true

items.prompt: In the line “Several planters thereabouts had attempted it on a commercial scale, in former years, with greater or less success; but like most Southern industries, it had felt the blight of war and had fallen into desuetude.”, what does “desuetude” most nearly mean?
options: a long speech by one person
lazy and lacking ambition
frames of crossed strips on which climbing plants grow
a state of disuse; no longer being used or kept up

items.prompt: In the line “The vines—here partly supported by decayed and broken-down trellises, there twining themselves among the branches of the slender saplings which had sprung up among them—grew in wild and unpruned luxuriance, and the few scattered grapes they bore were the undisputed prey of the first comer.”, what does “trellises” most nearly mean?
options: lazy and lacking ambition
a long speech by one person
a state of disuse; no longer being used or kept up
frames of crossed strips on which climbing plants grow

items.prompt: As used in the story (“Several planters thereabouts had attempted it on a commercial scale, in former years, with greater or less success; but like most Southern i”), what does “desuetude” mean?
options: a state of disuse; no longer being used or kept up
a feeling of fear of embarrassment
the process of taking a dispute to court
frames of crossed strips on which climbing plants grow

items.prompt: As used in the story (“The vines—here partly supported by decayed and broken-down trellises, there twining themselves among the branches of the slender saplings wh”), what does “trellises” mean?
options: gave; passed on
frames of crossed strips on which climbing plants grow
richly sweet and delicious
lazy and lacking ambition

items.prompt: As used in the story (“The estate had been for years involved in litigation between disputing heirs, during which period shiftless cultivation had well-nigh exhaus”), what does “shiftless” mean?
options: a person or thing equal to another in value or measure or force or effect or significance etc
in a warm, welcoming way toward guests
lazy and lacking ambition
a long speech by one person

items.prompt: As used in the story (“As he became more and more absorbed in the narrative, his eyes assumed a dreamy expression, and he seemed to lose sight of his auditors, and”), what does “monologue” mean?
options: the process of taking a dispute to court
a state of disuse; no longer being used or kept up
a feeling of fear of embarrassment
a long speech by one person

items.prompt: As used in the story (“After a little patient investigation, necessary to overcome the child's shyness, we learned what we wished to know, and at the end of about ”), what does “shyness” mean?
options: a feeling of fear of embarrassment
richly sweet and delicious
frames of crossed strips on which climbing plants grow
gave; passed on

shortAnswer: Explain how slavery and its memory develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how storytelling as resistance develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how race and economics develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the story's central concerns (slavery and its memory, storytelling as resistance, race and economics) and argue how the ending reframes it.

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what The Goophered Grapevine teaches about slavery and its memory. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Charles W. Chesnutt develops slavery and its memory in The Goophered Grapevine. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Charles W. Chesnutt develops slavery and its memory across The Goophered Grapevine. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of The Goophered Grapevine (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of slavery and its memory. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of slavery and its memory in The Goophered Grapevine. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Charles W. Chesnutt's choices in The Goophered Grapevine (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of slavery and its memory, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places The Goophered Grapevine's treatment of slavery and its memory in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on slavery and its memory in The Goophered Grapevine that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on slavery and its memory in The Goophered Grapevine. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about slavery and its memory in The Goophered Grapevine, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on slavery and its memory in The Goophered Grapevine, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
